blocks.text: Didymus, Geoponica book 15 [ch. 3, §. 7]: Θέλγει δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ζῶον, καὶ κάλλιστον μέλος· ὅθεν οἱ μελισσουργοὶ διασκορπιζομένας αὐτὰς κυμβαλίζοντες, ἢ τὰς χεῖρας εὐρύθμως κροτοῦντες συνάγουσι· [Thelgei de touto to zōon, kai kalliston melos; hothen hoi melissourgoi diaskorpizomenas autas kymbalizontes, ē tas cheiras eurythmōs krotountes synagousi] This animal is also charmed by the sweetness of song. Hence beekeepers gather scattered bees by striking cymbals or clapping their hands in rhythm. Against these the Philosopher is cited in vain, as though in the first book of the Physics he asserted that bees lack hearing. For I find the passage they cite nowhere. Indeed, in History book 9, ch. 40, he says that they are roused to work in the morning by a sound, and in the evening are called back from work by another sound, so that they may settle down [III, 360] to rest. Ὄρθριαι, he says, σιωπῶσιν, ἕως ἂν μία ἐγείρῃ βομβήσασα δὶς, ἢ τρίς· τότε δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἔργον ἀθροαὶ πέτονται· καὶ ἐλθοῦσαι πάλιν, θορυβοῦσι τὸ πρῶτον. κατὰ μικρὸν δ᾽ ἧττον, ἕως ἂν μία περιπετομένη βομβήσῃ ὥσπερ σημαίνουσα καθεύδειν· εἶτ᾽ ἐξαπίνης σιωπῶσι· [Orthriai … siōpōsin, heōs an mia egeirē bombēsasa dis, ē tris; tote d' ep' ergon athroai petontai; kai elthousai palin, thorybousi to prōton. kata mikron d' hētton, heōs an mia peripetomenē bombēsē hōsper sēmainousa katheudein; eit' exapinēs siōpōsi] In the morning they are silent until one rouses them by buzzing twice or three times. Then they fly out to work all together. When they return, they at first make a din, but gradually less and less, until one, flying around, buzzes as if giving the signal to sleep; and from then on they are at once silent. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 10: At night they rest until morning, when one rouses them with a double or triple buzz, as with a trumpet. Likewise: When evening comes, they hum in the hive less and less, until one flies around with the same buzz with which it roused them, as if ordering them to take rest, and this in the manner of a military camp. Then suddenly all fall silent. Yet, to state the matter as it is, the Philosopher had shortly before left the question uncertain in these words: Δοκοῦσι δὲ χαίρειν αἱ μέλιτται καὶ τῷ κρότῳ. διὸ καὶ κροτοῦντές φασιν ἀθροίζειν αὐτὰς εἰς τὸ σμῆνος, ὀστράκοις τε, καὶ ψόφοις. ἔστι μέν τοι ἄδηλον ὅλως, εἴτε ἀκούουσιν, εἴτε μὴ, καὶ πότερον· ἢ δι᾽ ἡδονὴν τοῦτο ποιοῦσιν, ἢ διὰ φόβον. [Dokousi de chairein hai melittai kai tō krotō. dio kai krotountes phasin athroizein autas eis to smēnos, ostrakois te, kai psophois. esti men toi adēlon holōs, eite akouousin, eite mē, kai poteron; ē di' hēdonēn touto poiousin, ē dia phobon] Bees also seem to delight in clapping. For this reason they are said to be gathered into the hive by the sound of brass or earthenware. Yet it is entirely uncertain whether they hear, and which of the two is the case: whether they do this from pleasure or from fear ^{(4)}.

In Deut. I, 44. Moses says of the Amorites, whom the Israelites had found the most hostile of all the Canaanites: They pursued you כאשר תעשינה דבורים, as bees do. So most of the ancients. But the Syriac renders it very differently: They pursued you, as bees ܡܬܬܢܢܢ that are smoked (or provoked by smoke) pursue an intruder. And the Arabic manuscript which I saw in Sweden: فطردوكم كما يطرد النحل بالدخان [fa-ṭaradūkum kamā yuṭrad al-naḥl bi-l-dukhān] And they drove you out, as bees are driven out by smoke. The Chaldee Onkelos too should be read thus: כמא דיתנן דבריתא, as one who smokes bees. For the word דנתון, which they twist in various ways, admits no suitable sense. These translators, evidently, seem to have read instead of תעשינה thaasena, that is, they do, תעשנה theassenna, that is, they are smoked: a slight change in the letters, and not an unsuitable sense. For it is well known that those who take the honey from hives first drive the bees off with smoke. Hence the poet, Georgics book 4, line 230:

— — and hold out in your hand pursuing smoke. [III, 361] And there Servius: Also bring smoke, so that, when the bees have withdrawn, frightened by these things, you may gather the honey with impunity. Likewise: Pursuing smoke, that is, the pursuers of the bees, as in and Malea's pursuing waves. And Ovid, De remedio Amoris book 1, line 185:
What of when swarms flee the smoke set beneath them, so that the honeycombs, removed, may lighten the curved wickerwork?
And Zonas, on Pan, to the bees, Anthology book 1, ch. 60:
— — — ὁ δὲ βλυστηρίδι χειρὶ [col. 508] Καπνώσας, βαίην κὔμμι λίπῃ μερίδα. [ho de blystēridi cheiri kapnōsas, baiēn kymmi lipē merida]
But may he, raising smoke with his honey-taking hand, leave you a small portion (of the honey). And of Aristaeus, Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 5, line 249:
Καὶ δολίῳ πνιγόεντι πυρὸς τεχνήμονι καπνῷ Σινομένην πρήϋνεν· — — — [Kai doliō pnigoenti pyros technēmoni kapnō sinomenēn prēynen]

And with the crafty, choking, skilful smoke of fire he calmed the harmful (bee). There are others too who report the same. Antigonus, History of Marvels 37: Τὰς δὲ μελίττας θυμιωμένας ὑπὸ τοῦ καπνοῦ, καὶ κακοπαθούσας τότε μάλιστα μὲν ἐσθίειν· [Tas de melittas thymiōmenas hypo tou kapnou, kai kakopathousas tote malista men esthiein] Bees (they say), when they are fumigated with smoke and harassed, then eat most of all. The Scholiast of Aristophanes, on these words of the Poet in the Wasps:
— — — Τῦφε πολλῷ τῷ καπνῷ, [Typhe pollō tō kapnō]
